Is anyone having this error when using Picocontainer with a constructor having a String?\n\3 satisfiable constructors is too many for 'class java.lang.String\

@alayor that's PicoContainer saying \I don't know what string to pass in here - let me see if I can construct one myself from the other  components I know about. And then it blows up because it has too many choices. Did you consider where that string constructor argument would come from?

@aslakhellesoy  I have a model class which has a constructor with a String parameter. I am trying to inject this object in some of the steps. In fact something similar happens with most of the wrapper types in Java (Integer, Boolean, Double, Character).   I think the class PicoFactory could provide constructors by default for this type of parameters.
I wonder if you want me to create an issue and provide a PR with a solution.
I don't think pico should make up primitive values to satisfy your constructors. Provide empty constructors instead, delegating to your string constructor.

[REFERENCE] I understand your point and as you mention correctly in your comment in the issue I opened, maybe this shouldn't be a PR to picocontainer.
However, picocontainer provides functionality to specify parameters for a particular class ([MutablePicoContainer.java](https://github.com/picocontainer/PicoContainer2/blob/master/pico/container/src/java/org/picocontainer/MutablePicoContainer.java)).
I think this functionality is to prevent this kind of problems when multiple constructors are satisfiable. Shouldn't we make use of this functionalty?

It is true that `MutablePicoContainer` allows specifying constructor parameters for certain constructors. The intention was always that this functionality should only be used to control how your _own_ classes are instantiated. In other words, it's ok to use it if you are also in control over the classes it's used against. In practice I never passed parameters to `addComponent`, I prefer default constructors instead. In any case, it would be wrong for Cucumber to make assumptions about what primitive values to pass into the constructors of _users'_ classes (classes we don't own). Aren't you able to define a default (empty) constructor to the class in question instead?

Designing your own fonts is crazy indeed when handling all those languages.

Performance does come into it. The loading of glyphs from disk happens on a background thread to avoid stalling the render thread, but there is a few ms where there is no glyph to display. You usually wait for all glyphs to load before displaying the text so you don't get partial words displayed on screen.
For this reason we would precache common glyphs at launch.
We would have all the glyph ABC data loaded into memory (dimensions, leading, etc) so we could always calculate text size. It was the glyph bitmap data that was loaded on demand.

I think it works the same as in Linux. I added `set(BUILD_SHARED_LIBS ON)` at the start of the CMakeLists.txt file and ran cmake in the root folder and then make
set(BUILD_SHARED_LIBS ON) will make all add_library definitions that don't specify the type explicitly make a shared library rather than a static one
I also added the -fPIC flag to the CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS and CMAKE_C_FLAGS. That way the compilers makes the code position independent so it can be used in a dynamic lib.
And lastly I had to wrap the code inside glsl_optimizer.h inside an `extern "C"`block so it conforms to the C ABI just like it's done inside PR aras-p/glsl-optimizer#135 in the source repo.

@tomspilman Sounds good. A short overview: /n/nThe parser I'm writing thinks in statements and blocks rather than words or tokens. You can specifiy which separators end a statement and delimit a block, but for now I think we only need a semicolon and braces. A block has a header and a body which is a collection of statements. The top level is a special kind of block without a header. Every block header and statement is classified based on string filters you set on the parser. You can easily add platform-specific rules in this step. After the parsing you can run through the hierarchy and pull information out based on the text in the statement. That means for example that you can only register samplers and textures when you're in the top level or inside a cbuffer/tbuffer, but not when you're inside a function. Here's an example to show the syntax for adding classification rules:/n/nIn the `AddClass` function, the first argument is the class you're adding, the second argument the filter. It should return true if a string belongs to the class you're registering. Third is the class of the block in which to use this rule, if omitted the top level block is assumed. You can pass multiple block classes if you want./n/n```/nparser.AddClass(StatementClass.Technique, s => s.FirstWordIs("technique"));/nparser.AddClass(StatementClass.Pass, s => s.FirstWordIs("pass"), StatementClass.Technique);/nparser.AddClass(StatementClass.VertexShader, s => s.FirstWordIs("VertexShader"), StatementClass.Pass);/nparser.AddClass(StatementClass.PixelShader, s => s.FirstWordIs("PixelShader"), StatementClass.Pass);/n/n// render state/nparser.AddClass(StatementClass.AlphaBlendEnable, s => s.FirstIdentifierIs("AlphaBlendEnable"), StatementClass.Pass);/nparser.AddClass(StatementClass.SrcBlend, s => s.FirstIdentifierIs("SrcBlend"), StatementClass.Pass);/n.../n/nif (<we're parsing a GLSL file>)/n    parser.AddClass(StatementClass.InputChannel, s => s.FirstWordIs("attribute"));/n```/nI'm adding utility functions (like `FirstWordIs`) that make writing these classification filters as easy as possible.

That is what we currently do for DXT only, and it was for compatibility at first with loading XNA XNB files on mobile platforms before we had our own content pipeline.  We only do DXT decompression at load time because a) XNA compressed textures were always DXT, and b) it is a known compression format.  The idea behind the content pipeline is that it compresses to a format that is supported by the target platform.  DXT on desktop platforms, PVR on iOS, ETC1/BGRA4444 on Android, etc.

Mesa is the odd one out here.  It is a software implementation of OpenGL, and it doesn't support DXT because of fears about the patents that S3 hold over the format.  Which would also be a reason to remove DXT decompression from our codebase.

Mesa is never used by devs or game players for developing or playing games.  @hach-que is using it for unit tests on a Linux build machine that has no GPU or display.  This is definitely an edge case scenario that is not supported.

and you can unbind that engine hook if you wish

@nkast could we enforce limitations for shaders when compiling shaders? XNA did this check for shaders during compile time.
@zigzag312 I don't know if it's possible, I am not familiar with the shader compilation code. @Jjagg ?
XNA content pipeline checked for this with the content project graphicsProfile, then during loading it checked the XNB file if it's build for Reach or Hidef.
I don't really like this approach because it has limitations on what we can do with the pipeline (think adaptive XNBs) and also in monogame it';s possible to load MGFX files directly from a stream.
@Jjagg , I think the shader compiler preprocess/parse the shader file to read some info, is that right? is it possible to get the technique from there?

2MGFX reads the techniques and passes. It then passes the shader profile to the compiler. The technique blocks themselves are removed before sending the code to the compiler because it's legacy effects framework syntax. So 2MGFX knows what shader profile is targeted.
MG's built effects are already incompatible with XNA's effects, so we might as well add the profile in.

I'm thinking about why XNA actually needs to know the graphics profile when building content... One thing I can think of is that meshes can only be indexed by shorts under Reach, so large meshes could fail under Reach while they could be successfully built under HiDef. There's probably more stuff like that. I don't know how much sense passing a graphics profile to MGCB.exe will make if MG will allow setting caps (rather than a full profile) in the future...
AFAIK MG does not currently use the GraphicsProfile when building content, but it's been a while since I touched content pipeline code so I might be wrong.

Great, so 2MGFX can include the shader model version in the file and then check that when MG loads it. Or we can have a 2 stage check, throw an error on compile time and then check the XNB  profile. however I don't think that MBCB passes the profile down  to 2MGFX.
No, 2MGFX does not take a graphics profile

Hey guys, decided to give Amber a try today. But so far it's not been smooth. I've been getting into issues all morning. It looks we have a bug with the YAML settings at the moment.

Creating a new application using `amber new blog -d pg -t slang -m crecto` and then starting it using `amber watch` gives the following error `instance variable '@uri' of Crecto::Repo::Config must be String, not (String | Nil)`.

The [Crecto](https://github.com/Crecto/crecto) `uri` must be of type `String`. But since settings are read from our defined YAML environment there's a type mismatch. In [settings.cr:15](https://github.com/amberframework/amber/blob/master/src/amber/environment/settings.cr#L15) we see that `database_url` defined as `String`. On the other hand, [settings:40](https://github.com/amberframework/amber/blob/master/src/amber/environment/settings.cr#L40) we see that the YAML macro  defined `database_url` as `String?` and defaults to `nil`. I assume that's why the type is reported as `String | Nil`.
I'd be happy to submit a PR for this. Just want to make sure we're doing the right thing here. If we can assume that the `database_url` always be set, I'd just remove the default value of `nil`.
If not, maybe defaulting to an empty string is more reasonable?

I'm very much in favour of a "language official", extendable task runner CLI tool, as opposed to every framework implementing their own set of CLI tools. Premier example would be 'mix' (Elixir) where each framework/tool/technology is free to define additional 'mix tasks' specific to that framework/tool/technology.
If one were to be inspired by `mix` behaviour, commands would look like/n```/n$ shard amber.run/n$ shard amber.watch/n$ shard amber.db.migrate/n$ shard amber.gen.scaffold/n```

It's one of the neatest CLI toolchain paradigms I've come across so far. In particular since dependencies of your app can freely extend these task sets, for instance, a testing dependency may introduce `mix coveralls.html` to produce a code coverage report in HTML format.

Is there a distinction between a mountable app that you mount inside an amber app and a plugin that provides the same functionality?  I think there isn't.  You want a mountable app to provide calendar services for your amber application.  A plugin (once we implement the plugin feature) could generate many artifacts, models, views, controllers, migrations and as Faustino points out the artifacts could be contained within a module using the modular paradigm.  Fundamentally the mounted app or plugin provides routes, actions and views but there may also be database migrations.   If we can also declare routes, sockets, pipes, channels and everything else we create for the parent application, within the module, then this would be a mountable app to all intents and purposes.  The modular paradigm is the way to go with everything connected with a route prefix contained within the module.  Adding features, mounted apps, plugins - whatever we call them would simply be a case of generating a module from the desired plugin template.

@vifreefly Hi!  Crystal does not have threads but it does have fibers and channels. https://crystal-lang.org/docs/guides/concurrency.html
this is similar to Go on how to handle concurrency.
To handle parallelism, you currently need to use `port_reuse` and run multiple processes.

I have a stupid question regarding how to change/build aws-sdk-go. I'm new to go, so bear with me. In the repo, I have a sneaking suspicion that this file might come from some other source? apis/dynamodb/2012-08-10/api-2.json
I'm asking because there's a ScalarAttributeType in that json file - that governs the attribute types for DynamoDB, and that type does not include 'M', just 'S', 'N' and 'B'

Hi @hngkr Those API json files define what API operations are available and the Input/Output structures for them. Generally these definition files are shared between each language's AWS SDKs. In this case, `ScalarAttributeType` is an enumerable string type which can take the values M,S,N or B. These are available as constants in `dynamodb.ScalarAttributeTypeS`,  `dynamodb.ScalarAttributeTypeM`, `dynamodb.ScalarAttributeTypeN`, and `dynamodb.ScalarAttributeTypeB`.
In order to ensure backwards compatibility with API's the enum's type is not used and string constants are created instead in the pattern of {Type}{EnumValue}

The Reason `M` is not being accepted is because ScalarAttributeType requires scalars such as numbers, strings, or boolean types. M represents Map is not a scalar
Are you looking to set a Hash or Range key, or create a scheme for table? Those values can only be scalars types, Maps are not valid types for those.
Creating a schema - nothing fancy with hash/range keys. It seems possible in Boto3, but not in the NodeJS API.

Generally you shouldn't need to create a scheme for records unless they are intended to be searchable with hash or range keys.

[REFERENCE] Hello all!  I am just wondering what needs to be done to move the proposal for Date and Time types along?  Would it help if I put a proposed implementation together?  Are more scenarios and use cases required?  Any other ideas?
@mj1856  Can I just ask a question: are there any obstacles for using noda time? i.e. why do people want to have this in CoreFx repo?

Sure.  I am a huge fan (and contributor) of Noda Time.  Some of the obstacles are the common ones with any external library:  learning curve, adoption, beurocratic approvals, etc.  But besides that, there's some friction to overcome with participating in the rest of the .NET ecosystem.   We end up having to write adapters, such as NodaTime.JsonNet, NodaTime.RavenDB, NodaTime.Dapper, etc...   And there are some areas like EF that make it imposible to even go about writing an adapter.   If there were some sort of lower-level API for data type mapping that Noda Time could hook into, things would be much cleaner.  But there isn't.
At a more practical level, having types for `Date` and `Time` separated from `DateTime` would align much better with SQL Server's `date` and `time` types.

It would also help with serialization.  The recommended way to serialize this stuff with JSON or XML is via ISO8601.  That's fine, but a lib like JSON.Net has no way to know you want `2015-03-05` instead of `2015-03-05T00:00:00`.  There are indeed differences between those two. :)

Also there is just a matter of trying to be more complete and accurate.  Currently .Net does things like DateTime.Today which just sets the time to midnight, but glosses over the fact that midnight *might not exist* within the local time zone, such as in Brazil on the day of the spring-forward DST transition.
I guess it boils down to - we'd like .NET to "do the right thing", out of the box.  Noda Time can do more advanced things, but it shouldn't be needed to do things "correctly".
`Date` and `Time` vs `DateTime` is something I also wanted a few times in the past, so +1 for figuring out the best way here :)

BTW, I fully understand the benefits of noda time (or more generally separation betwen time, dates, etc.). I am specifically asking for what prevents people from simply using noda time when they have a need for such separation. To this, if I can summarize, you provided several good points I understand: adapters (somethine clunky, sometimes not working), approvals, and some I don't undersatand: learning curve (to me the learning curve is the same no matter where the API lives).

Just so you guys know, these are some of the dillemas we have with cases like this one: a) we don't want to do "us too" library if there is an existing good library in the community, b) for many library additions we considered in the past, we concluded that they add value for, let's say, 20% of customers, and add complexity for the other 80%. In such situation, we are more inclined to say that such library should be "out of band", i.e. not built in. The 20% of people who need it, can opt into using it. But the 80% who don't need it, don't have to deal with the complexity. This of course results in the "adapter" problem, but I have to say I have not found a clean way to solve it. Possibly, because we have not tried hard enough. Maybe now is the time.

I hear you about the "us too" point.  One could envision a System.Time namespace, nuget package, etc. with all the stuff Noda Time has, then folks would be scratching their heads on which library to use.  So I'm not suggesting a full merge of ideas into the corefx.   Certainly NodaTime.ZonedDateTime is opinionated, and would create more headache than it's worth.  I'd say the same thing for Period, Instant, IClock, and other items in NodaTime.

However, at the same time, I don't think .NET should gloss over things that are incorrect.  It's fundamentally wrong to coerce date-only or time-only into a `DateTime`.  Sure, it reduces the API surface, and there's less to learn.  But it comes at the expense of creating potential for errors in the data.
So the proposal is more about moving the line over a little bit, rather than going all one way or the other.
Besides, the argument about having too many classes is a bit silly IMHO when you consider how many different collection types we have that are special purpose.  If we can do it there, why not here?

I don't think making a small change here is worth it. It won't solve the problems for the 20% of developers who are not happy with DateTimeOffset and will just add a bit more complexity to it. I am very much interested in making a big dent for the 20% of developers (without hurting the 80%). Right now, I think the best shot at this is to fix general probblems that people have with using out-of-band (OOB) libraries. For example, can we do something in CoreFx that will make adapters more succesful? Can we do something in serializers, such that serializers (either these in CoreFx or community ones) work with such OOB libaries?

What could be done to make adapters more successful?   Well, for one thing, anywhere that has a big case statement of data types could be refactored to be pluggable by interface or convention. No, for a few reasons:
1. As an actual **time span**, the definition of years/months/days is irrelevant to hour/minute/second definitions.

2. Date spans are usually to be interpreted in the calendar on which they're used, so you need to convert one or both to the same calendar (which will usually include time zone, too).  The resultant 'period' may be calendar un-aware, depending (there are a few different uses).
A big part of the problem is that there are multiple definitions for 'date and time', depending on use.  If I say I want to call you at 3PM, there's a few problems:
1. My time zone, or yours?
2. What happens if either one of our offsets change - do we keep the original 'absolute' (UTC) time, or the 'relative', 'local' time?
If I want to get "everything that happened yesterday", what do I really mean?
1. Everything that happened in my local calendar 'yesterday'?
2. Everything that happened in the last 24 hours?
3. Everything that happened 'yesterday' for UTC?
yeah and some more predicaments in server-client, domain-based and such environments.
You can't really deal with this by just making one type that can be culture-aware or not, you actually want different, narrow-specification, types for each definition/use

You are right, given the complexity, we cannot have one normalization/abstraction layer, which translate all kinds of calendar/time inputs to UTC and then DateTime, TimeSpan etc. make use of it. There are many parts of .NET that rely on date/time functionality in the BCL, and wouldn't be able to easily depend on Noda Time or any other alternative library.  For example, consider the ADO.Net data type mappings that are used when you pass a `DateTime` or `TimeSpan` into SQL Server.

I can see a good use case for `ConfigureAwait(true)` (ie. force this to always run on the main thread and not in the thread pool, to avoid any possibility of race conditions if you're running multiple async tasks) but why would you ever want to force the opposite to happen?
You're asking why you'd want to use `ConfigureAwait(false)`? http://blog.stephencleary.com/2012/02/async-and-await.html#avoiding-context
It's an expensive bottleneck that interferes with execution order unnecessarily.

In my case, it ended up running CPU-heavy code and freezing the UI thread even though I invoked the original method with `Task.Run` to start it off on a background thread. As soon as the first `await` continues, it's off the background thread and back on the UI thread.
Wait, then why are you using `await`s on CPU-bound code?

@masonwheeler ConfigureAwait(true) doesn't force it to always run on the main thread. It simply uses the current SynchronizationContext. As @jnm2  points out, using the current synchronization context is often a bad idea. Framework code (as opposed to application code) should always use ConfigureAwait(false).

Async for web service calls, sync for SqlDataReader.
I see
Plus some actually CPU-heavy work.

And I've tested it on some  pretty script-heavy stuff and never noticed a performance bottleneck from that.

[REFERENCE] You do need a `SynchronizationContext` — check out the issue I opened about this.
@masonwheeler That's what I meant.
Someone had to have set up a SynchronizationContext, or your ConfigureAwait(true) calls would still be going to the thread pool.
@wekempf is right. If you don't install one, this happens: https://github.com/dotnet/csharplang/issues/97#issuecomment-322681371
Yeah, I'm pretty sure that's getting taken care of when the window that the game plays in is created.
`new System.Windows.Forms.Control()` installs one.
What you have in that game is a "chatty" cooperative synchronization situation. That can perform very well if your tasks are short, but when they aren't you can get into some real performance issues.

If [`WindowsFormsSynchronizationContext.AutoInstall`](http://referencesource.microsoft.com/#System.Windows.Forms/winforms/Managed/System/WinForms/WindowsFormsSynchronizationContext.cs,11ce7ff2c55ebd9d,references) is true, which it is by default.
How so?
Also, do you mean if the tasks are short, or if the individual snippets of code being executed between `await`s are short?
Code you expect to be running asynchronously isn't. :)
because I've done a lot of work to make sure the latter is true
@masonwheeler You're doing everything on one thread, so anything that blocks (whether IO or CPU) means nothing else is running.
The snippets of code between awaits *are* tasks. :)
It's the difference between multi-tasking and cooperative multi-tasking. :)
@jnm2 Yeah, that's why I did a bunch of work to ensure that blocking stuff isn't ever running synchronously
That's interesting, but that works.
I assume you `Task.Run` the blocking stuff?

It's much more work, but if you can do everything correctly via cooperative multi-tasking you can actually perform better (you eliminate the need for context switching). But, in general, most code will run better when you ConfigureAwait(false) when you don't need to be back on the SynchronizationContext.
Once you `Task.Run`, anything inside will act as though you have `ConfigureAwait(false)`.
Anyway, you don't need two people. @wekempf has it right. 😁
Any async I/O or other "threadless tasks" will be fine in his scenario. So, as long as there's no long CPU intensive operations he wouldn't even need the Task.Run.
@wekempf Right.

The full set of rules is/n```/nFor the pow function (integral exponents get special treatment):/n    pow (x, ±0) is 1 for any x (even a zero, quiet NaN, or infinity)/n    pow (±0, y) is ±∞ and signals the divideByZero exception for y an odd integer < 0/n    pow (±0, −∞) is +∞ with no exception/n    pow (±0, +∞) is +0 with no exception/n    pow (±0, y) is +∞ and signals the divideByZero exception for finite y < 0 and not an odd integer/n    pow (±0, y) is ±0 for finite y > 0 an odd integer/n    pow (±0, y) is +0 for finite y > 0 and not an odd integer/n    pow (−1, ±∞) is 1 with no exception/n    pow (+1, y) is 1 for any y (even a quiet NaN)/n    pow (x, y) signals the invalid operation exception for finite x < 0 and finite non-integer y./n```

The full set of rules is/n```/nFor the pow function (integral exponents get special treatment):/n    pow (x, ±0) is 1 for any x (even a zero, quiet NaN, or infinity)/n    pow (±0, y) is ±∞ and signals the divideByZero exception for y an odd integer < 0/n    pow (±0, −∞) is +∞ with no exception/n    pow (±0, +∞) is +0 with no exception/n    pow (±0, y) is +∞ and signals the divideByZero exception for finite y < 0 and not an odd integer/n    pow (±0, y) is ±0 for finite y > 0 an odd integer/n    pow (±0, y) is +0 for finite y > 0 and not an odd integer/n    pow (−1, ±∞) is 1 with no exception/n    pow (+1, y) is 1 for any y (even a quiet NaN)/n    pow (x, y) signals the invalid operation exception for finite x < 0 and finite non-integer y./n```

and the CoreFX results all match up with that/n`pow (x, ±0) is 1 for any x (even a zero, quiet NaN, or infinity)` covers the first/n`pow (x, y) signals the invalid operation exception for finite x < 0 and finite non-integer y.` covers the second/n`pow (+1, y) is 1 for any y (even a quiet NaN)` for the third/n`pow (−1, ±∞) is 1 with no exception` for the fourth and fifth

The C Runtime standard has a few more rules on-top of that, which we also adhere to (mostly because we are implemented in terms of the CRT math functions, but also because they match the broader IEEE spec as well):

```/nF.10.4.4 The pow functions/n— pow(±0, y) returns ±∞ and raises the ‘‘divide-by-zero’’ floating-point exception for y an odd integer < 0./n— pow(±0, y) returns +∞ and raises the ‘‘divide-by-zero’’ floating-point exception for y < 0, finite, and not an odd integer./n— pow(±0, −∞) returns +∞ and may raise the ‘‘divide-by-zero’’ floating-point exception./n— pow(±0, y) returns ±0 for y an odd integer > 0./n— pow(±0, y) returns +0 for y > 0 and not an odd integer./n— pow(−1, ±∞) returns 1./n— pow(+1, y) returns 1 for any y, even a NaN./n— pow(x, ±0) returns 1 for any x, even a NaN./n— pow(x, y) returns a NaN and raises the ‘‘invalid’’ floating-point exception for finite x < 0 and finite non-integer y./n— pow(x, −∞) returns +∞ for | x | < 1./n— pow(x, −∞) returns +0 for | x | > 1./n— pow(x, +∞) returns +0 for | x | < 1./n— pow(x, +∞) returns +∞ for | x | > 1./n— pow(−∞, y) returns −0 for y an odd integer < 0./n— pow(−∞, y) returns +0 for y < 0 and not an odd integer./n— pow(−∞, y) returns −∞ for y an odd integer > 0./n— pow(−∞, y) returns +∞ for y > 0 and not an odd integer./n— pow(+∞, y) returns +0 for y < 0./n— pow(+∞, y) returns +∞ for y > 0./n```

Changing the underlying type of a public or protected enum is the worst kind of binary breaking change possible./nIf someone uses your enum type in an attribute argument, their assembly can't be parsed or loaded properly unless the loader can locate your assembly and find the underlying enum type (by type name serialized as a string), and then read that many bytes of the attribute data. If the assembly was compiled against a version of your assembly that used `: byte` but runs/is parsed against a version of your assembly that uses `: int`, the loader will read four bytes instead of one and mess up parsing all the attribute arguments following that (and probably crash when it reads too far).

I'm unhappy that assemblies are not completely parseable without resolving referenced assemblies./nIt complicates every time I have to parse attribute data with all kinds of complex concerns. It requires an understanding of how to resolve assemblies in the same folder as the assembly being parsed as well as how to resolve its target framework assemblies.

[REFERENCE] Besides knowing how to resolve assemblies the way the assembly expects, this requires the assembly loading work that was proposed to actually read the located assembly, or else something home-brewed. I've been doing home-brewed stuff in every project so far... it's monotonous.
This weakness is inherent to the ECMA-335 spec itself, so it's not going away anytime soon.

Btw: the reason for using SafeHandle/CriticalFinalizerObject (which contain finalizers) versus a writing a finalizer yourself:/n/n- Stronger runtime-enforced safety guarantees when with finalizers/n- Scopes the finalization to precisely the things that need it rather than the whole managed class which uses the handle, making it harder to shoot yourself in the foot/n- Can log failures to release

(The managed class should dispose the SafeHandle deterministically, but it doesn't need a finalizer or Dispose(bool). If someone drops the managed class on the floor, the SafeHandle still gets finalized and the unmanaged resource freed.)

> but what if that doesn't create a valid object? Is there no way to prevent that?/n/nThere is no way to prevent it. `default(Foo)` is legal on any type and it means "set all the bits in the storage location to zero."
For reference types, setting all the bits in the storage location to zero gives you a null reference. For a value type, it zeroes all the fields of the struct.
Also, the storage memory of arrays and class fields and static fields are zero-filled by the CLR.
With `new FooStruct[100]`, the storage for the struct fields lives in the array. All instances start out as `default(FooStruct)`.
There are two general approaches: detect uninitialized memory and throw, like ImmutableArray does, or do whatever is necessary to make a zero-filled fields a valid representation of something.
The CLR forces all types to be defaultable, and especially with generics, it's too late to change that. Rust makes you opt in: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/default/trait.Default.html

@jnm2 yes, to something user defined
Since zero-fill is a function that the CLR performs, you'd need a new CLR and your library would crash on all runtimes and versions that exist today.
Because existing runtimes would keep zero-filling because they don't know about anything else.

Hey, a fellow `System.Data.SqlClient` hacker. Are you planning on going anywhere near `SqlBulkCopy`, by any chance? Because I am. :-)

I have no plans to go near it but if someone gives me a profile-able test case i could. Mostly i'm just investigating things that i find while trying to be efficient so there's no real plan just whatever turns up.

I'm currently looking at all the ways it's slower than just running `bcp`, with an eye towards fixing that so managed code is at least on par. That involves comparing it against a real SQL Server; I don't know if your tests also do that or whether they're restricted to shuffling stuff in memory.

speed is largely limited by the TDS protocol itself from what i've seen. You can make it work quicker ot idle but end to end timing increases seem unlikely. I've been working mostly on memory and efficiency gains with a few bug fixes throw in. I've got 7 pr's ongoing at the moment of which i think the oldest might help bulk copy, i tightened up the rpc allocation bahaviour.

[REFERENCE] Speed *should* be limited by TDS, but it's not -- that's my whole beef. Things ought to be I/O bound, but I'm hitting CPU bounds way before that, and straightforward bcp and SSIS both beat .NET code unless you take real good care. For starters, there's an old issue about the missing ORDER hint which prevents streaming rows in order, which (fortunately) is relatively easy to fix. After that, I'll see.
I have noticed that even just using .NET Core instead of .NET Framework gives notable speedups, which is encouraging, but even then it still lags behind bcp.

That's not even mentioning that `SqlBulkCopy` seems designed to give you the slowest possible perf out of the box, what with its default options being to not do a table lock, encourage you to use the incredibly inefficient `DataTable`, etc. That can mostly be solved by properly using the class, although there are opportunities for copying data more quickly there too.

If you need to change the api, which i think you do for that, then you'll need to put together an api change request. That doesn't mean you can't do the work up front but you'll need to go through the process to get approval.
Fastest isn't always best.  I use bulk copy on live tables where TABLELOCK would definitely be a bad thing.

As i said if i've got something that runs for long enough to profile and benchmark, say 30s or so, i'm quite happy to investigate stuff. I'm learning a lot through this process and hopefully improving sqlclient for most consumers while i'm at it.
I just really hope you aren't using your app on linux

Yes, there are scenarios where `TABLOCK` would not be appropriate. I won't make any case for changing the existing defaults; the backwards compat breakage would not be worth it anyway. I can bitch and moan about the decisions of `SqlBulkCopy` separately, but I don't propose changing any of that.
> I just really hope you aren't using your app on linux/n/nI'll bite, what's the problem there? :-)
checkout the profiler screenshots https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/pull/35363
Egads. No, this particular app can run comfortably on Windows for the moment. Definitely something to consider for other scenarios, though.

On windows you're pretty safe. it'll use the pinvoked library that the main framework has been using since the beginning and that's pretty well tuned for perf. you're still stuck with weird things going on in the managed layer but some of that can be mitigated once you understand where your problem actually is.

My scenario comes very close to basically blitting a TDS rowset into another channel that would accept that same rowset... the theoretical minimal overhead is very small, but I'll easily settle for just being *reasonably* I/O bound, albeit I/O bound on some hideously fast SSDs.
We're talking a very big partitioned table, so this can (and will) easily exploit parallelism, but that presumes an efficient way to do it for just one thread for starters.

you should already be io bound on the network. if you've bumped up your packet size as high as you can you shuld be waiting on ack from the server side for the packets. I've not seen a write limited profile so far though so i've no idea if there's any fat that can be cut there.

I should be; not the case at the moment, for various reasons, the missing `ORDER` hint being one. But yeah, I don't expect to squeeze much out of the I/O layer beyond that. I am using the max packet size already. If you want to see SQL Server itself stumble, though, just make it read a really wide table. For whatever reason, the optimizer has a real problem maximizing throughput when you do that. Fortunately just spamming cores and issuing a lot of `SELECT`s in parallel helps.
I forgot about the whole native network layer below; I'm definitely not going to dive further into that one -- unless I've *really* got too much time on my hands.

you can't. the native dll is closed source. If you want to change the network layer you'll have to do it on the managed version. The problem with the managed version is that it's nowhere near as fast and you can't enable it on windows (Because of the speed disadvantage) so it's only currently usable on private builds or unix
Yes, I meant diving into it as in looking at the managed/unmanaged interface and changing the managed bits. ...although the unmanaged bits being closed source is disappointing.
the two interfaces are separated out in the TDSParserStateObject, looks at the managed vs native versions to see what it does. That pr i linked earlier makes changes to the managed one.

I have the feeling (but can't back it up with strong assertions) that there's still quite a bit of room for improvement on the networking level, even taking the unmanaged + native combo as a baseline, which starts to matter more when your server's faster (think in-memory OLTP). For now I'll just focus on my bulk copy. :-)

the protocol is the limitation from what i can see and the way around that is paralellism as you've said. you've got to wait on getting data from the disk, wait to send and wait to ack before you can prepare the next packet. you can't prepare ahead because the state and packet numbers need to be correct. The managed networking implementation is slower than the native one so there might well be work that can improve that
if you've got the tools and the will though it'd be good to see what you can find and possibly improve

TBH there's probably something to be said for overhauling TDS itself to squeeze out these last drops of performance for very big/very quick transfers, but that's above the pay grade of this repo. For now SQL Servers can mostly still expected to be disk I/O bound so I see why it's not a big priority.
the in-memory stuff might see a benefit, though
in-memory stuff?
Yes, but in-memory is already such a big boost compared to disk (while retaining SQL compat) that people aren't likely to complain soon. :-)
Anyone who's not satisfied with that speed now has probably looked at SQL alternatives already, rather than getting a few % more from in-memory. Still, potentially worth looking at.

Hey folks, I've got another API design question. So when `ValueTask<T>` was first introduced it was 'just' a union of a `T` and a `Task<T>` the idea being to make methods that frequently completed synchronously allocation free. Neat!/n/nBut then they added `IValueTaskSource<T>`, which made things all wonky. If i understand correctly, IVTS is for things that produce **sequential** async operations. The API uses some for of magic to reuse whatever allocation the Task(?) requires from for each await. Making the entire await loop allocation free. Right? The caveat is that now ValueTask<T> is more fiddly and has special rules such as it may not be awaited more than once or by multiple awaiters. /n/nIf this is correct, do we know why the BCL folks didn't add a new `SpecialValueTask` or something that created a clear separation of behavior between normal `ValueTask<T>`s backed by T or Task<T> and special `ValueTask<T>`s backed by IVTS?

IVTS can be used for sequential things but I think the more obvious purpose was to allow a thing to be it's own awaitable. if you look at the changes to http2stream that went in recently it was optimised using ivts so that when you await the stream the stream itself is the thing you're awaiting and it knows it's finished by signalling internally so there are no/fewer allocationcations and no external source.
usually If you lookup the apo proposal for these things you'll find a good deal of explanation
Hmm, couldn't you already be your own awaitable by implementing `GetAwaiter()` and  `ICriticalNotifyCompletion`?
@AlgorithmsAreCool i think they enhanced `ValueTask` just so they could have one unifying "standard" async interface.

Makes sense, I figured they were walking a line between too many different concepts and concept complexity. I was just wondering, because now I kinda avoid returning ValueTask<T> because my API consumers have to treat it with kid gloves.
do you listen to the api reviews that they broadcast on youtube at all? because the topic of how to choose between task and valuetask came up a couple of weeks ago
I sometimes do, but they are usually over an hour and don't have summaries. So i can't always devote the time to listen.

if you can find it it's somewhere in the json review stuff. I think the gist of it was use valuetask if you know that the majority of the time the call will return synchronously but if there is any doubt just use task

@sameerkattel It is a reference assembly, an assembly that does not contain implementation of the API, but describes the API shape.
When you compile an application against CoreFX libraries you compile against those reference assemblies. The compiler sees all the classes and methods that the assembly should implement.
However when you run your application it loads the actual implementation assembly.
You may ask...why have two? Why not use the same one for both compilation and actual execution?

Well, one of the reasons is that there is usually more than two. The implementation may be different between platforms (Linux, macOS, Windows) and some assemblies also have implementation for full .NET Framework on Windows.
During compilation it is verified that the implementation assembly matches the API specified by the reference assembly.
(during the CoreFX compilation, that is)

@Wraith2 Here's an oversimplification of what await does./n/nAwait is syntax sugar:/n/n```cs/nasync Task FooAsync()/n{/n    Console.WriteLine(await GetIntAsync());/n}/n```/n/nFor something like the following (which is oversimplified for demonstration purposes)./nNote *when* GetAwaiter, IsCompleted, OnCompleted, and GetResult are called and *why*:/n/n```cs/nTask FooAsync()/n{/n    var source = new TaskCompletionSource<object>();/n/n    var fooAwaiter = GetIntAsync().GetAwaiter();/n    if (!fooAwaiter.IsCompleted)/n        fooAwaiter.OnCompleted(FooAsync_Part2);/n    else/n        FooAsync_Part2();/n/n    return source.Task;/n/n    void FooAsync_Part2()/n    {/n        Console.WriteLine(fooAwaiter.GetResult());/n        source.SetResult(null);/n    }/n}/n```

Specifically, OnCompleted is never called by `await` unless IsCompleted has returned false. GetResult is never called unless either IsCompleted initially returned true *or* OnCompleted invoked the callback.

ConfigureAwait(false) returns an object whose awaiter schedules the OnCompleted delegate on the thread pool after the task completes./nConfigureAwait(true) returns an object whose awaiter schedules the OnCompleted delegate via SynchronizationContext.Current.Post after the task completes./nA task object's awaiter behaves the same as the ConfigureAwait(true) object's awaiter.
Therefore if OnComplete doesn't end up getting called, ConfigureAwait is irrelevant.
YieldAwaiter has IsCompleted always return false so that OnCompleted must be called, and then OnCompleted immediately calls SynchronizationContext.Current.Post to execute the delegate.

In reality, `await` is lowered to [something a lot more complex](https://sharplab.io/#v2:EYLgxg9gTgpgtADwGwBYA+ABADAAgwRgG4BYAKGz3wFYTSyMBmPAJhwGEyBvMnXnABygBLAG4BDAC4w8SADxCAdhIB8OAOIwJASSUBBAM4BPBWAAUAShwBeVQBMYAMzEBXADYTaPPhgAcMnABiEBAGxmbmXrzcpHyxlACcphjx6po6EqEmFua0sQC+ZAWkQA) which is more general, handles exceptions, etc, and does it more efficiently./n/nBut the intuitions are still valid around `await` decomposing to the GetAwaiter, IsCompleted, OnCompleted, and GetResult calls as shown in my example.

ValueTask is a union of three possible backing states:/n/n- synchronously-obtained value, no Task ever allocated/n- Task instance to represent an asynchronous wait: traditional, heavy-weight, used to be the only option for async waits/n- IValueTaskSource (+ hidden ushort token) to represent an asynchronous wait: no Task, allocs are no longer per-ValueTask but instead can be amortized to ~zero.

There were times where I wished that one or other class was not `sealed` but it was not because of deliberate design. There were generally two reasons for that.
Reason one, the code had a bug and unsealing would offer an opportunity for a workaround.
Reason two, I wanted to attach additional data to existing class that was internally used by other component. (Objective C has this concept, btw)
yes, it was used in the recent zero day they discovered

And, of course, often it was combination of both reasons when trying to solve incorrect design. We had to do that with `HttpWebRequest` and certificate validation callbacks. Until NetFX 4.5 the certificate validation callback was global. You got reference to the `HttpWebRequest` that needed the validation but you could not attach additional data to it. This made it nearly impossible to propagate something like `CancellationToken` through those old APIs. We first used workarounds with thread-static variables around `HttpWebRequest` calls but it breaks once you start using the `Begin/End` async APIs...

@aadamsx I know, but you will want to know that your tools will allow you to scale efficiently, both in terms of resources and cost.

@niallobrien: Meteor will scale... there are options.  One precaution I took upfront is to build an app per client (and each client will have there own customers).  But I didn't make this choice based on scale alone.  There's a lot of other factors to consider.  Such as customization requests from users (one-offs), usage (customer that uses more, should pay more, and I should scale them differently in some cases) -- why build an elaborate scaling system for everyone (that could come with performance drawbacks) when only one or two clients call for it for example.  Backup solutions, if I have all my clients in one DB (most efficient), and one client wants to hold onto there data, man that's going to be a pain to have to pull out there data from the rest -- if they have their own db -- easy.  I could go on, but I'm ok with this solution based on the rate of return.  Yes, there will always be a better way, better toolset, but in the end if you're not making money then none of it matters.

There is something I would like to share regarding the process of putting the app on FDroid, I myself have been trying a lot to put the SUSI.AI app on FDroid, but there are several problems in between. PSLab Android app is successfully put on FDroid , the reason being it did not use any proprietary software and further all the open source software that was used was from trusted source, SUSI now has two build flavors one for FDroid and other for Play-Store, so similarly the app here should be made into two build flavors if any proprietary software is used.

SUSI has hotword detection libraries that use binary files which being open source still are not acceptable by FDroid, furthermore when you build the app for FDroid you must just build the FDroid flavor

and that is again a blocker for me, though I am constantly trying putting app on FDroid , but I am majorly stuck , even though you do not use any proprietary software there are still certain restrictions which must be taken care of just like for the binary files for hotword detection

@jphastings when a user navigate between routes, before rendering the next screen the router should be able to load all the required data for a particular screen only then render the screen.. e.g. with [react-routing](http://www.kriasoft.com/react-routing) and `history` libraries it may looks something like this:/n```/nimport Router from 'react-routing/src/Router';/nimport http from './core/http';/nimport Location from './core/Location'; // an instance of the `history` module/n/nconst router = new Router(on => {/n  /n  on('/some-page', async (state) => {/n    const data = await http.get('/api/some-data');/n    return data && <SomePage {...data} />;/n  });/n/n});/n/nLocation.onChange(async (location) => {/n  await router.dispatch(location, component => {/n    React.render(component, document.body);/n  });/n});/n```

what i did was /n- make a branch A from my master/n- rebase it on top of RSK master/n- resolve all conflicts painfully until everything works/n- take another branch B off my master/n- merge RSK master into my master/n- have a bunch of conflicts/n- replace source tree of B with A with a straight copy/overwrite to resolve the conflcits/n- abandon branch A, commit B/n- merge B back to my master/n
the reason for doing this wacky procedure was that it's much easier to understand the changes while doing an interactive rebase
but your commit history will be a bit bizarre if you merge the rebase back to your master because your old commits look like 'new' on top of a history that already has those commits
so you get a commit history in master that looks like you did a merge

Well first of all adding the config in webpack:/n```/nconst clientConfig = extend(true, {}, config, {/n  entry: {/n    home: './entries/home.js',/n    error: './entries/error.js',/n  },/n.../n    // Extract all common chunks/n    new webpack.optimize.CommonsChunkPlugin('commons', 'commons.[hash].js'),/n```

After that you need to allow the routes to be able register the bundle they want to use/n```/n///n// Register server-side rendering middleware/n// -----------------------------------------------------------------------------/napp.get('*', async(req, res, next) => {/n  try {/n    let css = [];/n    let statusCode = 200;/n    const template = require('./views/index.hbs');/n    const data = { title: '', description: '', css: '', body: '', commons: assets.commons.js };/n/n    if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production') {/n      data.trackingId = analytics.google.trackingId;/n    }/n/n    await match(viewRoutes, {/n      path: req.path,/n      query: req.query,/n      context: {/n        insertCss: styles => css.push(styles._getCss()),/n        setTitle: value => (data.title = value),/n        setMeta: (key, value) => (data[key] = value),/n      },/n      setBundleJs: bundle => (data.entry = assets[bundle].js),/n      render(component, status = 200) {/n        css = [];/n        statusCode = status;/n        data.body = ReactDOM.renderToString(component);/n        data.css = css.join('');/n        return true;/n      },/n    });/n/n    res.status(statusCode);/n    res.send(template(data));/n  } catch (err) {/n    next(err);/n  }/n});/n```

[REFERENCE] @/all there are some breaking changes in the PR I just merged:
- The `history` npm module has been upgraded to v4.x having different API ([changelog](https://github.com/mjackson/history))
- The layout markup and styles have been extracted from the `App` component, see [App](https://github.com/kriasoft/react-starter-kit/blob/master/src/components/App.js), [Layout](https://github.com/kriasoft/react-starter-kit/blob/master/src/components/Layout/Layout.js).
- Updated `client.js` and `server.js`
- The route components now explicitely specify the parent (container) component, for example:
  `class AboutPage extends Component { render() { return <Layout>….</Layout>; } }`

In general, it’s not a good idea to specify view hierarchy inside the route declarations, it’s better to do that inside React. At a first glane, it might look like code duplication (specifying the outer (container) component in each route/view component), but it’s very simple mental model, very easy to understand how it works and it’s super powerfull. You can always remove code duplication by creating another container component, for example, you can create ProductLayout component on top of the basic Layout component, and include side menu, breadcrumbs etc. then use that inside your Product route/view component - “render() { <ProductLayout>…</ProductLayout>; }" instead of the basic Layout component.

Hallo! I already mentioned that our company wants 4 more shops on base shuup. So is possible manage several shops on one database ? I mean, other settings, other themes, order and product management per shop? If yes, how to do that?

[REFERENCE] @soulilya It is possible, yes, but partially. You can check the issue I've linked about the multi-shop limitations. So, at this very moment, it is possible to create multi shops in same database, but they shouldn't be able to configure there own order status, product types and other models that don't have `shop` as an attribute. Without that, all shops have access to the same objects and that could lead to some issues (battling for changing them). So, depending on your project requirements, I recommend you to check all models that don't have the `shop` and check if that is required to be per-shop object, if so, you have to create a new database for each shop. Now, creating a new DB for each new shop will require you to have new settings and probably new http server workers.
Adding the `shop` on every object will probably solve this. We were adding those in past weeks and there is still some models lacking of that.
